analysis.one_liner: Caps malpractice payouts and lawyer fees, and shields FDA-approved drugs from punitive damages.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to two House committees in February 2009, never received a hearing or a vote, and died when the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would set nationwide rules for medical malpractice lawsuits, overriding state laws where those are more generous to injured patients. It would cap payment for pain and suffering at $250,000 per case (money for lost wages and medical bills would stay unlimited), shorten the deadline for filing a claim, cap what lawyers could charge on contingency, make each defendant pay only its own share of fault, and ban punitive damages against any drug or device the FDA had approved. Sponsors argued this would lower malpractice insurance costs and reduce wasteful 'defensive medicine'; opponents say it caps what catastrophically injured patients can recover.
analysis.who_benefits: Doctors, hospitals, and drug and device manufacturers would face sharply lower malpractice exposure: damage and lawyer-fee caps, a shorter filing window, and no punitive damages for FDA-approved products. Medical malpractice insurers would pay out less. Patients with minor injuries and low economic losses would see little change; the caps bite hardest on those with catastrophic, non-fatal injuries.

how_it_helps.text: Caps non-economic damages — payment for pain and suffering — at $250,000 per case, regardless of how many defendants or claims are involved.
Shortens the window for suing to one year after discovering an injury or three years after it appeared, with narrow exceptions for fraud, concealment, or a foreign object left in the body.
Bars punitive damages against makers of FDA-approved medical products, and shields prescribers from being named in product-liability suits over such products.
Caps lawyer contingency fees on a sliding scale (40% of the first $50,000 down to 15% above $600,000) and lets juries hear that the patient's insurance already paid some bills.
Makes each defendant pay only its own share of fault and allows future damages to be paid in installments rather than up front.

analysis.who_pays: Patients seriously injured by medical negligence or unsafe medical products — especially those whose main loss is pain, suffering, or a death in the family rather than lost wages — would see their recoveries capped at $250,000 for non-economic harm, and could not seek punitive damages for injuries from FDA-approved products. State courts would lose the power to set their own rules.

drawbacks.text: It caps compensation for pain, suffering, disfigurement, and loss of a loved one at $250,000 no matter how severe the injury — a fixed ceiling that hits children, stay-at-home parents, and elderly people hardest, since they have the smallest economic losses to recover.

It bars punitive damages against any drug or device the FDA approved, and shields doctors who prescribe it from product-liability suits — even when later evidence shows the product was dangerous, unless the company hid information from the FDA.
It preempts state law, overriding the damage rules and patient-protection laws that individual states have chosen for themselves whenever a state's rules are more generous to injured patients.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill promised lower malpractice insurance premiums and possibly lower health costs by making lawsuits cheaper to file and harder to win. But its main guaranteed effects were to cut what injured patients could collect — a hard $250,000 ceiling on pain-and-suffering damages, a near-total bar on punitive damages against FDA-approved products, stricter filing deadlines, and lower attorney fees — while the hoped-for savings for patients through lower premiums or less defensive medicine were speculative and would depend on insurers and providers passing them on. The costs to people catastrophically injured by malpractice would be certain and concentrated on them; the benefits diffuse and unguaranteed.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Judiciary and Energy and Commerce committees and its health subcommittee, was never scheduled for a vote, and expired when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 13, 2009 and referred to the House Judiciary Committee and the Energy and Commerce Committee the same day.
Ten days later it was referred to the Judiciary Committee's Health Subcommittee; that was the last action ever taken on it.
No hearing, markup, or floor vote occurred, and the bill died when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.
It had 72 cosponsors, all but two of them Republicans.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Plaintiffs' trial lawyers keep the current system, and injured patients keep full access to state courts; malpractice insurers and providers avoid the new caps but also get no federal relief from lawsuit costs.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Plaintiffs' bar and injured patients' court access

for.name: Phil Gingrey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and organized 33 original cosponsors.

for.name: House Judiciary and Energy and Commerce Committees
for.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral; neither scheduled a hearing or markup, so it never advanced.

sides.party_line_note: 72 of the 74 cosponsors were Republicans (70 of 178 House Republicans, 2 of 253 House Democrats), and with Democrats controlling both chambers and the bill never reported from committee, it drew no floor action.

industries.note: Caps on noneconomic damages, punitive damages, and attorney fees would directly cut the payouts these insurers must make, reducing their exposure. Their argument that savings pass to patients as lower premiums would be unverified by this bill.

Malpractice premiums are a major cost for providers, and the bill would cut both their liability and the lawsuits they face. Patients harmed by negligence would give up much of their remedy in exchange.

The bill would bar punitive damages against any product the FDA approved or cleared, effectively capping their worst-case liability to judgments on individual claims. Patients harmed by such products could still recover economic damages but not punitive ones.

Fee caps and damage caps directly reduce what contingency lawyers can earn and which cases are worth bringing. Because they represent injured patients rather than an industry, their loss tracks the loss to patients.
